lessons.title: Expected points
lessons.objective: You can say what EPA measures without a math degree.

payload.prompt: EPA (expected points added) measures what?

options.text: How much a single play changes the team's expected scoring probability
The total yards gained in a game
The quarterback's salary

explanation.correct: EPA is a predictive stat. Every play moves the needle on what the offense will likely score from that field position.
explanation.incorrect: EPA is not about yards or money. It measures how much each play helps or hurts the team's scoring chance.

payload.prompt: A 10-yard gain on first and 10 from midfield has how much EPA?

explanation.correct: A 10-yard gain on first down from midfield is a good drive continuation—roughly 0.4 points added. The offense is now much closer and has four downs left.
explanation.incorrect: Field position and play type matter. A 10-yard gain early in a drive gains about 0.3 to 0.5 EPA depending on starting position.

payload.prompt: A quarterback with a high EPA per play is playing better than one with low EPA, all else equal. True or false?

scene.alt: A quarterback with high EPA per play, improving his team's expected scoring on each snap.

explanation.correct: True. Higher EPA per play means the QB is creating more value on every snap. It is one of the best indicators of quarterback performance.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, EPA per play is one of the most predictive stats for quarterback quality.

payload.prompt: Match each stat to what it tells you.

pairs.definition: How much value each play adds to the offense's expected score.
The share of plays that keep the offense on schedule (40% of needed yards on first, 60% on second, all on third).
Together they show if an offense is both efficient (EPA) and consistent (success rate).

explanation.summary: EPA is value created per play. Success rate is consistency. Both matter.
explanation.sayThisLine: High EPA? Efficient. High success rate? Reliable. Both? Elite.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: His EPA per play is elite, but his success rate is below average. He is getting yards, just not consistently.

payload.question: What is the analyst saying?

options.text: The player is playing great all around
The player creates value per play but is inconsistent; some plays are huge, some fail
The player should be benched
The player is not a good fit for this team

payload.translation: A high EPA with low success rate means explosive plays mixed with stalls. The offense is streaky, not steady.

followUps.line: Is a high-EPA, low-success player good or bad?
followUps.why: Tests understanding: both stats matter. Explosive plays are valuable but inconsistency is risky.

followUps.line: What would make this player elite?
followUps.why: If he adds both EPA per play (efficiency) and consistency (success rate), he is a superstar.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about the difference between 'good plays' (EPA) and 'reliable plays' (success rate).

lessons.title: The go-for-it revolution
lessons.objective: You can explain why analytics pushed fourth-down aggression.

payload.prompt: Fourth and two, down by three, two minutes left. Analytics say go for it. Old school says punt. Who is right?

options.label: Go for it
options.consequence: Analytics show go-for-it has better win probability than punt. If you get two yards, you live. If you miss, game is still likely lost.
considerations: EPA models show going for it at four and two has higher win probability than punting.
You need a touchdown anyway, so field position is secondary.
The offense is hot; strike now.

options.label: Punt and hope
options.consequence: Punting is safe but it lowers your win probability. Analytics changed this calculus.
considerations: Punting has been the default for decades.
But the math now favors going for it in most fourth-down situations.
Fear of failure is why coaches still punt.

payload.expertNote: Fourth-down analytics is the biggest coaching revolution in 20 years. Modern teams go for it more often because the math says it wins more games.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: Analytics say we should have gone for it on fourth and three last week. We would have won.

payload.question: What is the coach saying?

options.text: Analytics are always right
The numbers show going for it increased their win probability more than punting
Fourth down is always a go-for-it
The defensive line played badly

payload.translation: The expected-points model says trying for the conversion would have given them a better chance to win than punting.

followUps.line: Does analytics say always go for it on fourth down?
followUps.why: No. Context matters: score, time, field position, down and distance all change the math.

followUps.line: Why do coaches still punt if analytics say go?
followUps.why: Tests your understanding: fear, tradition, and not trusting the model sometimes overrule the math.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think: analytics weigh the risk of losing the ball against the benefit of keeping the drive alive.

payload.prompt: Why did analytics change fourth-down strategy?

options.text: The math showed that going for it has higher win probability than punting in many situations
Running backs became faster
Defenses could not tackle as well

explanation.correct: EPA models showed that punting surrenders too much value. Going for it, even with modest conversion rates, often improves win probability.
explanation.incorrect: The analytics revolution is about win probability, not physical talent. Better modeling changed strategy.

payload.prompt: A team that goes for it more often on fourth down should win more games, all else equal. True or false?

scene.alt: A team going for it on fourth down and converting, improving their win probability.

explanation.correct: True. Going for it when the math favors it improves expected win probability. Over a season, this compounds.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, the teams that adjusted fastest to go-for-it analytics won more in the 2020s.

payload.prompt: At what conversion rate does fourth and one become a better bet than punting?

explanation.correct: Around 55% conversion rate, going for it on fourth and one has higher win probability than punting. At 50%, it is breakeven.
explanation.incorrect: The threshold depends on score, time and field position, but roughly 55% is the breakpoint for fourth and one.

lessons.title: Are running backs worth it?
lessons.objective: You can argue both sides of the running back debate.

payload.prompt: The running back value debate is about whether?

options.text: RBs deserve big contracts given short careers, injuries, and easy replacement by committee or younger backs
RBs should wear different uniforms
The running back position is not important

explanation.correct: Teams now ask: is paying a star RB $10M a year worth it when a veteran minimum back and a young backup can do 80% of the work? The debate is about cap allocation.
explanation.incorrect: The debate is really about money and value. Star running backs are expensive and have short peak years.

payload.title: The running back contract argument
payload.setting: Debating a friend on whether your team should pay a star RB.

exchanges.theirMessage: We should sign that running back. He is the best in the league.

replies.text: He is great, but can we afford him and still build the rest of the team?
replies.theirResponse: That is fair. We are cap-strapped already.
replies.coachNote: Shows you know salary cap matters more than talent alone.

replies.theirResponse: He is, but is it worth it?
replies.coachNote: Agreeing is fine. Add a follow-up about the tradeoff next time.

replies.text: RBs are easy to replace with committee backups anyway.
replies.coachNote: Over-reaching. Some backs are generational. Ask about value, not dismiss the position.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: Yes, he is elite. But his career arc is steep and short. By year four of a five-year deal he will be a backup, and you are still paying like he is elite.

payload.question: What is the analyst saying?

options.text: Elite running backs never decline
Running backs decline quickly; you might overpay for years when they are not producing
The player should be cut immediately
Running backs should make more money

payload.translation: The running back position has a steep learning curve (starts young) and early decline (peaks around 25-28, falls off by 30). Contracts often extend past the peak.

followUps.line: Why do running backs decline faster than, say, quarterbacks?
followUps.why: Tests understanding: RBs rely on burst and quickness; QBs rely on intelligence and accuracy, which age slower.

followUps.line: Is this debate just about running backs?
followUps.why: It is similar for other positions: receivers, edge rushers. But RB decline is steepest and most predictable.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about the age curve of a typical running back versus other positions.

payload.prompt: Sign a star RB to a five-year, $50M deal, or build depth with veteran backups?

facts.label: Needs
facts.value: Offense needs help at multiple spots

options.label: Build depth with cheaper backs
options.consequence: A committee of younger and veteran minimum RBs can handle 90% of the production at 20% of the cost. Use the cap elsewhere.
considerations: Modern teams have moved toward committee backs.
Cap efficiency matters more than star power at RB.
With $50M, you can fix multiple holes.

options.label: Sign the star RB
options.consequence: Elite talent does matter. But you sacrifice flexibility for other positions and are vulnerable to injury.
considerations: A true elite RB is still a weapon.
You are limited elsewhere on the roster.

payload.expertNote: The RB value debate is really about cap allocation. Modern economics favor depth and flexibility over one expensive star at a position with easy replacement.

payload.prompt: A committee of veteran backups can often replicate 85-90% of a star RB's production at 20% of the cost. True or false?

scene.alt: Multiple running backs sharing carries, achieving solid production without a star player.

explanation.correct: True. The RB position benefits from fresh legs and is less reliant on a single standout talent than WR or QB.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, this is the core of the modern value debate. You can build a productive RB room without breaking the cap.

lessons.title: The quarterback wins myth
lessons.objective: You can say why quarterback wins is a shaky stat.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: His record is 120-90, so he must be one of the top winning quarterbacks ever.

payload.question: What is wrong with this logic?

options.text: Records are a team stat, not a QB stat. Defense, kicking, and running game matter a lot
He obviously never won anything
Records do not mean anything
He is not a real quarterback

payload.translation: Quarterback wins (the QB's record) credits wins entirely to the QB, but team wins are a team statistic. The defense, running game, coaching and luck all matter enormously.

followUps.line: Can a great QB on a bad team have a losing record?
followUps.why: Yes, absolutely. A Hall of Famer on a weak team can go 8-9. A mediocre QB on a great team can go 12-1.

followUps.line: What is a better stat than QB wins?
followUps.why: EPA per play, yards per attempt, touchdown-to-interception ratio, decision-making in clutch time. Any stat that isolates QB performance.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about a great QB on a bad team versus a mediocre QB on a great team. Who has the better record?

payload.prompt: Why is a quarterback's win-loss record misleading?

options.text: It credits everything to one player when wins depend on offense, defense, special teams and coaching
Quarterbacks do not actually affect games
Records are kept incorrectly

explanation.correct: A QB can play great and lose, or play poorly and win. Wins are a team outcome, not a QB outcome.
explanation.incorrect: QB wins is a surface stat. Deeper stats like EPA, yards per attempt and TD-to-INT ratio isolate individual performance.

payload.prompt: A quarterback with a 90-70 record is automatically better than one with an 85-75 record. True or false?

scene.alt: Two quarterbacks with different win-loss records, showing that team composition matters.

explanation.correct: False. The 85-75 QB might have done more with less (worse team). Record alone does not show individual quality.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, context matters. One QB might have had a better team around him.

payload.prompt: Someone argues a QB with a 105-60 record is better than one with 95-70. How do you counter?

options.label: Explain team context
options.consequence: You show that QB A played on great teams while QB B played on weak ones. Record is misleading without context.
considerations: Defense matters hugely to team wins.
Same-era defenses are not equal.
Better context = better argument.

options.label: Quote EPA or yards per attempt
options.consequence: Comparing individual stats works, but requires knowing those numbers.
considerations: Individual stats are cleaner than records.
Not everyone knows EPA.

options.label: Agree that records matter
options.consequence: You lose the argument if you concede that wins are a pure QB stat.
considerations: Winning matters, but team wins do not isolate QB play.

payload.expertNote: QB wins is a trap stat. Always contextualize with team defense and offense quality before comparing records.

payload.prompt: Match each stat to whether it isolates QB performance.

pairs.definition: Team statistic; heavily influenced by defense, running game and special teams. Misleading for comparing QBs.
Isolates QB efficiency. One of the best indicators of individual QB performance.
Isolates QB decision-making and arm talent. Less affected by defense than wins.

explanation.summary: Use individual stats to compare QBs, not records. Records tell you about the team.
explanation.sayThisLine: Wins are about the team. EPA is about the QB. Compare apples to apples.

lessons.title: Tush push and the kickoff
lessons.objective: You can explain two live rule fights.

payload.prompt: Fourth and one. Your QB sneaks with teammates pushing. Illegal or genius?

facts.label: Fan reaction
facts.value: Half say genius, half say unfair

options.label: It is legal, so it is fair game
options.consequence: The rule book says it is legal. Teams that exploit it win more on short yardage. That is football evolution.
considerations: The ban vote failed 22-10; 32 teams could not agree it was wrong.
If it is legal, use it.
Fans will argue, but the league has ruled.

options.label: It is nearly unstoppable and should be banned
options.consequence: A reasonable opinion. The play does seem to violate the spirit of individual competition.
considerations: Some fans feel the assist defeats the purpose of short yardage.
But defenders could also push to stop it.

payload.expertNote: The tush push is a perfect example of a rule debate: legal but controversial. The 2025 ban vote failed because teams are split on fairness versus innovation.

payload.title: The tush push and kickoff debates
payload.setting: Debating rule changes with a friend who has opinions.

exchanges.theirMessage: The tush push is ruining football. It should be banned.

replies.text: I get it. Some love the creativity, others think it breaks the spirit of short yardage. What would you ban?
replies.theirResponse: Just that one play. Everything else is fine.
replies.coachNote: Shows you understand both sides and respect her view.

replies.text: It is legal though, so it is fair.
replies.coachNote: True, but it does not end the conversation. Acknowledge the debate.

replies.text: That rule is fine, stop complaining.
replies.coachNote: Dismissing her opinion ends the conversation. Show curiosity instead.

payload.prompt: The tush push controversy is really about?

options.text: Whether a sneak with an assist is unfairly powerful or creative innovation
Whether the quarterback should wear padding
Whether short yardage plays should exist

explanation.correct: It is a fairness debate. Is the play so good it breaks short-yardage as a test, or is it brilliant design? Both sides are reasonable.
explanation.incorrect: The tush push is about whether the league will let this version of the QB sneak stand.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: The dynamic kickoff is too wild. We do not know what the rule will be next year. It kills tradition.

payload.question: What is the analyst worried about?

options.text: The kickoff is too dangerous even with the new rule
Rule changes make the kickoff unpredictable and tradition matters in football
Kickoffs are not important to the game
The league is broken

payload.translation: Football has traditions (the kickoff is over a century old), but the league keeps tweaking it for safety and entertainment. Some fans want consistency.

followUps.line: Is the dynamic kickoff safer than the old one?
followUps.why: Yes, statistically. But some fans hate that the league keeps changing it.

followUps.line: Will the kickoff rule keep changing?
followUps.why: Likely. The league will try different setups to balance returns, collisions and entertainment.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about what the analyst values: tradition or safety innovation.

payload.prompt: Rule changes every few years are necessary for safety, even if they disrupt tradition. True or false?

scene.alt: A kickoff play showing the evolution of the rule over time for safety.

explanation.correct: True. The kickoff is the most injury-prone play. The league has tweaked it repeatedly to reduce harm while keeping returns alive.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, player health is the league's stated reason for the kickoff changes.

lessons.title: Player safety and load
lessons.objective: You can talk about concussions and rule changes with respect.

payload.prompt: The concussion protocol is designed to?

options.text: Remove and clear a player after a suspected head injury, preventing return-to-play too soon
Make the game softer
Keep star players on the bench all season

explanation.correct: The protocol is a medical safeguard. A player is removed, checked by independent doctors, and must pass tests before returning.
explanation.incorrect: Concussion protocols are a player health measure, not a competitive tool.

statement.speaker: Player
statement.text: That hip-drop tackle was the only way to bring him down. Now it is 15 yards. The league is changing how we play defense.

payload.question: What is the player saying?

options.text: Hip-drop tackles are the best way to tackle
Rule changes eliminate techniques defenders have used, causing frustration
The league is targeting him personally
He is a bad tackler

payload.translation: The NFL banned hip-drop tackles starting in 2024 because of injury risk. Defenders now have to adjust their technique, which is difficult for veteran players.

followUps.line: Does banning a tackle technique actually reduce injuries?
followUps.why: Data suggest yes, though some defenders argue other tackles are equally risky.

followUps.line: Is it fair to change rules mid-career for veteran players?
followUps.why: Legitimate question. Players trained for decades in old techniques and now must retrain.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about a rule you grow up with suddenly becoming illegal.

payload.prompt: Reducing the number of practices and full-contact drills helps prevent injuries and overload. True or false?

scene.alt: Players recovering during reduced-contact practices, managing workload and injury risk.

explanation.correct: True. The league and teams now manage practice intensity to reduce cumulative head impacts and other injuries. It is an emerging safety frontier.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, practice contact reduction is part of modern player health management.

payload.prompt: A defender tackles a runner by dropping his hips and driving his legs. Hip-drop or wrap?

facts.label: Tackle type
facts.value: Swivel hips, drive legs into runner

options.label: Wrap technique instead
options.consequence: Wrap your arms around the runner's torso. Takes more practice but legal and generally safer.
considerations: Wrapping is the league's preferred technique now.
Defenders are retraining after years of hip-drops.

options.label: Use hip-drop (risky)
options.consequence: You get flagged and hurt your team. 15 yards is not worth the penalty and injury risk.
considerations: The rule is in place for a reason.

payload.expertNote: Rule changes feel awkward at first. Defenders who adapt fastest to wrap tackles thrive; those who cling to old techniques get flagged.

payload.prompt: Match each safety rule to what it addresses.

pairs.definition: Medical assessment and clearance after a suspected head injury; prevents early return-to-play.
Banned in 2024; defenders must use wrap or other techniques to reduce leg-driven impacts.
Forcible contact to the head or neck area of a defenseless player; automatic ejection if confirmed.

explanation.summary: Modern football prioritizes player health. Rules address head impacts, tackle technique and unnecessary contact.
explanation.sayThisLine: Concussion protocol: check a player. Hip-drop: change your technique. Targeting: no head shots.
